policies.summary: For a facility that needs a state certificate (25 MW or more, or storage of 25 MWh or more), failing city, county or airport zoning does not stop the Commission from issuing it, and once it issues no city, county or regulatory agency may require any further approval, permit or license for construction.

A generating plant or group of plants at a single site totaling 25 MW or more, or an electric storage unit of 25 MWh or more, needs a certificate of public convenience, use and necessity from the Iowa Utilities Commission; smaller facilities need no Commission certificate and are left to county and city zoning.

restrictions.description: Proposed 765 kV MISO transmission line, land negotiations in the Hebron area, and concern that data centers require large amounts of electricity and water. Active as of 2026-09-23. On Sept. 9, 2026 the Board repealed and rescinded Resolution No. 2026-45 (the Adair County Data Center Regulatory Ordinance) because the required public hearing had not yet been held; that did not affect the Resolution #2026-26 moratorium. A public hearing on the data center regulatory ordinance was set for 9:15 a.m. on 2026-09-23; its outcome was not yet reported at research time. The Board also set a $500 data center permit fee in August 2026. Legal basis: Resolution #2026-26, "Resolution to Establish a Temporary Moratorium on the Construction of Data Centers, High-Density Computing Facilities, and Battery Storage Facilities in the Unincorporated Areas of Adair County, Iowa," adopted March 18, 2026 by unanimous 5-0 roll call.

County has no specific ordinance for utility-scale BESS; time needed to coordinate with agencies and create ordinances. Extended; active as of 2026-09-23 through 2027-05-01 or earlier passage of a BESS ordinance. Legal basis: Resolution 2025-46 (2025-08-12); extended by Resolution 2026-25 (2026-05-05).

Planning and Zoning Commission needs time to draft ordinances covering infrastructure, natural resources and property rights. Active/extended as of 2026-09-23 (through Dec. 31, 2027) for all three categories. Legal basis: Resolutions 26-62 (data mining), 26-63 (utility-scale battery storage), 26-64 (data storage centers), extending prior 2026 moratoria.

Active as of 2026-07-31 if not extended; six months from 2026-05-12 would run to approximately 2026-11-12, and no extension or rescission was identified in the reviewed sources. Legal basis: Resolution 2026-8, barring the county from accepting applications or issuing building, use, zoning, or rezoning permits for data centers, bitcoin mining facilities, solar collection and storage facilities, and battery energy storage systems, for six months.

Board wants ordinances regulating construction, operation and decommissioning of utility-scale solar and battery storage (safety, neighbouring property, county roads) before any are built. Extended as of 2026-09-23; the USSES/BESS construction moratorium adopted 2025-01-28 has been continued three times, most recently by Resolution 26-28 (signed 2026-09-22), to 2026-12-31 at 11:59 p.m., while the county drafts solar and battery-storage zoning rules. Legal basis: Resolution 25-05 (2025-01-28), 'Temporary Moratorium on the Construction of USSES and BESS in the Unincorporated Areas of Emmet County, Iowa'; continued by Resolutions 25-36, 26-13 and 26-28.

County needs a BESS ordinance; BESS was not addressed in the new wind ordinance. Extended; active as of 2026-09-23 through 2026-12-29. The prior extension expired Aug. 4, 2026 (no BESS applications were filed during the gap) and the Board unanimously renewed it on 2026-09-15 while Planning and Zoning finishes proposed BESS regulations. Legal basis: Original November 2023 wind/BESS moratorium; Res #04-26 (2026-01-20) extending the BESS moratorium to 2026-08-04; Board action of 2026-09-15 extending it through 2026-12-29.

County has no ordinances for solar, BESS, data centers or data mining facilities and wanted policy in place before any projects are proposed. Active as of 2026-09-23; remains in place through 2026-12-31 while the county drafts solar, BESS and data center/data mining ordinances (public discussion held in September 2026). Legal basis: Henry County Board of Supervisors moratorium action of 2026-05-14 (instrument number not published in coverage).

County lacks a Utility-Scale Battery Energy Storage Systems ordinance; Planning and Zoning Commission needs time to draft one. Active/extended as of 2026-09-23, through Aug. 31, 2027. Legal basis: Resolution #1004-01-02-2024 (original); extended by Resolution #1063-09-10-2024 (to 2025-06-30) and Resolution #1157-12-23-2025 (to 2027-08-31).

Board sought time to review zoning rules before allowing data center and battery storage development. Active as of 2026-09-23 per statewide roundups (Radio Iowa July 8, 2026; KCCI Sept. 9, 2026 lists Madison County among places with temporary pauses in place); no repeal or replacement ordinance found. [VERIFY instrument number; primary source (news-only evidence) not confirmed at confidence 0.45 in the 2026-07 refresh]. Legal basis: Two Board of Supervisors ordinances (data centers; battery storage systems) adopted 2026-05-26 with second and third readings waived, per KCCI; ordinance numbers not published in the coverage reviewed.

Need to draft a utility-scale BESS ordinance. Extended; active as of 2026-09-23 through 2027-02-01 (or earlier BESS ordinance). Resolution No. 2-10-2026 (2026-02-10) renewed the BESS moratorium before the original term lapsed; the March 10, 2026 Resolution No. 3-10-2026 extended only the separate cryptocurrency/data-mining moratorium despite its motion line's ambiguous wording. As of the July 7, 2026 meeting, Invenergy was still asking the Board for a battery-storage ordinance, confirming no BESS ordinance had been adopted and the moratorium remained in force. Legal basis: Resolution No. 5-13-2025 (2025-05-13), original BESS moratorium to 2026-04-01; renewed by Resolution No. 2-10-2026 (2026-02-10), 'A Resolution Approving a Temporary Moratorium on Battery Energy Storage Systems,' effective immediately until 2027-02-01 or passage of a BESS ordinance.

Regulatory gap on siting large-scale data centers and industrial battery storage. Reported active as of the June 16, 2026 vote; not independently confirmed against a primary document in this pass. Legal basis: Board of Supervisors resolution (unanimous) placing a year-long moratorium on permitting large-scale data centers and industrial battery storage facilities; specific resolution number not located in this pass.

Shelby County has no existing ordinance governing siting, construction, and operation of commercial solar energy systems. Active as of 2026-09-23; Resolution 2026-14 runs through 2027-07-01 unless extended or superseded by an ordinance. Shelby County Board minutes for July 21, Aug. 18 and Sept. 1, 2026 record no ordinance adoption, extension or rescission for commercial solar energy projects. Legal basis: Resolution 2026-14, Moratorium on Solar Energy Construction Permits.

Shelby County has no existing ordinance governing siting, construction, and operation of commercial battery storage projects. Active as of 2026-09-23; Resolution 2026-15 runs through 2027-07-01 unless extended or superseded by an ordinance. Shelby County Board minutes for July 21, Aug. 18 and Sept. 1, 2026 record no ordinance adoption, extension or rescission for commercial battery storage projects. Legal basis: Resolution 2026-15, Moratorium on Battery Storage Construction Permits.

Shelby County has no existing ordinance governing siting, construction, and operation of commercial wind energy systems. Active as of 2026-09-23; Resolution 2026-17 runs through 2027-07-01 unless extended or superseded by an ordinance. Shelby County Board minutes for July 21, Aug. 18 and Sept. 1, 2026 record no ordinance adoption, extension or rescission for commercial wind energy projects. Legal basis: Resolution 2026-17, Moratorium on Wind Energy Construction Permits.

Board desired additional time to review Sioux County Ordinance No. 01 (the county's general land-use/zoning ordinance) before any data center or BESS project could be considered; the resolution notes no such facilities were installed or in development in the county at the time. Active as of 2026-07-31 (sunsets automatically 2027-06-16 absent further Board action). Legal basis: Resolution No. 2026-32, prohibiting the Board of Supervisors, Zoning Board, and Board of Adjustment from receiving, reviewing, considering, or approving any Data Center and/or BESS application, to allow time to review Ordinance No. 01.

County regulations were silent on digital asset mining, cryptocurrency operations, data processing centers, and battery/energy storage uses. Active as of 2026-09-23. Extended via Resolution #26-69 (adopted 2026-03-17) through 2027-03-31, covering digital asset mining, cryptocurrency operations, and data processing centers (BESS was moved to permanent Ordinance No. 330, adopted the same day). No further rescission or replacement found; a September 2026 statewide roundup still lists the moratorium as in place through March 2027. Legal basis: Resolution #25-97 (adopted 2025-06-17); extended via Resolution #26-36 (adopted 2025-11-25) through 2026-03-31; further extended via Resolution #26-69 (adopted 2026-03-17) through 2027-03-31. The same March 17, 2026 meeting adopted Ordinance No. 330 (third consideration), which permanently regulates battery/energy storage uses, spinning BESS out of the moratorium; the moratorium itself continues to cover digital asset mining, cryptocurrency operations, and data processing centers.

No ordinance for battery storage; concerns about fire hazards, safety risks, emergency response preparedness, environmental contamination, setbacks and visual impacts; agricultural preservation. Active as of 2026-09-23 (indefinite); no comprehensive plan, BESS ordinance or rescission found in Board minutes through Aug. 24, 2026. Legal basis: Resolution 11-10-2025B (Tama County Board of Supervisors, 2025-11-10).

Active as of 2026-09-23. Ordinance #40 was approved 3-0 on 2026-07-30 and runs twelve months from publication for data centers, solar energy systems (>50 kW or >1/2 acre), battery energy storage systems and mineral right development. Wind is not covered by Ordinance #40, and the Board approved the Black Maple Wind WECS permit application in late August 2026. Legal basis: Ordinance #40, "Taylor County Temporary Development Moratorium Ordinance" (temporary moratorium on acceptance, processing and approval of applications for data center, solar energy system, battery energy storage system and mineral right development), adopted 2026-07-30 under Iowa Code 331.301, 335.2 and 335.3; preceded by the 2026-05-07 amendment of Resolution 2023-21.

Clarke County, Iowa supervisors adopted Resolution #24-219 on Dec. 16, 2024 (3-0): a temporary moratorium on the construction of commercial solar panels in the unincorporated county, in place until the board imposes a permanent moratorium, passes an ordinance regulating them, or rescinds it.

Linn County replaced its utility-scale solar moratorium with siting rules in its Unified Development Code: solar equipment 300 ft from dwellings unless the owner waives it, 120 ft from perennial streams and ditches, 50 ft from property lines in the Renewable Energy overlay district; battery storage 200 ft from property lines and rights-of-way and 500 ft from off-site occupied structures unless waived; 55 dBA day and 50 dBA night noise limits; RE overlay rezoning and a passing score on the county's solar scorecard. Concentrating solar power is prohibited, and fenced arrays over 160 acres need a wildlife corridor.

In September 2024, Adams County adopted wind regulations that cap total wind turbines in the county to 225 turbines and require turbines to be set back at least 1.5 times turbine height from property lines.
In November 2019, the County’s Board of Supervisors capped the number of commercial wind turbines allowed in the county at 535 turbines.
Last amended in November 2022, Butler County’s zoning ordinance for unincorporated areas includes a number of restrictions on wind development.

In May 2023, the Cerro Gordo County Board of Supervisors passed a 15-month moratorium on utility-scale solar and wind energy, along with battery storage facilities, in order to consider regulations for future permitting of such facilities.
Since 2009, wind energy conversion systems, such as wind turbines and windmills, have been prohibited within the City of Council Bluffs.
On September 24, 2024, Clinton County’s Planning and Zoning Commission issued a three-month moratorium on commercial wind farm applications as they revised the county’s 2008 wind ordinance.

The county zoning ordinance provides that noise from wind turbines cannot exceed 30 dBA for any period of time when measured from any dwelling, school, hospital, church, or public library existing at the time of approval.
In March 2022, Greene County put in place a moratorium on utility-scale solar farms for either 6 months or until the Iowa legislature passes a law that addresses solar farms.
In May 2021, the Grundy County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 to pass an indefinite moratorium on wind farm construction in the county.
An indefinite moratorium on wind farms was implemented in the fall of 2019.
In October 2024, the Kossuth County Board of Supervisors adopted a 9-month ban on the processing of large-scale or utility-scale solar farm applications.

In April 2021, the Worth County Board of Supervisors adopted a moratorium on wind energy development until July 2022, at the same time as the developer Invenergy was in the process of obtaining easements for a 30,000-acre wind farm.

In August 2023, Woodbury County supervisors further amended the zoning ordinance to disallow utility-scale solar energy systems in agricultural protection districts, allowing them only in general industrial districts.

projects.description: Clenera Energy's 100 MW, 750-acre Coggon Solar project west of Coggon drew sustained opposition over prime farmland, property values and setbacks. The Planning and Zoning Commission voted 6-1 in late November 2021 to recommend denying the rezoning. After public meetings on Jan. 10, 13 and 18, 2022, the Board of Supervisors approved the third and final reading 2-1 on Jan. 24, 2022 (Walker and Rogers for, Zumbach against). The board removed, 2-1, the 950 ft soft setback and 28 in. panel-height conditions added earlier, and added a vegetative screening buffer within 1,000 ft of occupied residences and a decommissioning estimate without salvage value.
In August 2018, the Madison County Coalition for Scenic Preservation challenged Madison County’s decision to approve this 52-turbine wind farm.
Beginning in 2019, the developer of Coggon Solar began public outreach related to an application for a 640-acre, 100-MW solar project in Linn County.

projects.project_name: Duane Arnold Solar Projects I and II
projects.description: In 2022, Palo-area residents filed a lawsuit opposing the rezoning of land for two industrial-scale solar projects, claiming that the Linn County Board of Supervisors failed to follow county land-use policies and relied on illegal spot zoning to permit a renewable energy project near the decommissioned Duane Arnold nuclear plant.
A 3-turbine wind farm that was approved in 2015 and then constructed was taken down in 2018 following a successful legal challenge by residents.
In August 2015, the Black Hawk County Board of Adjustment unanimously voted to deny a special permit and setback variance for Optimum Renewables’ proposed 3-turbine, 6-MW wind energy project.
In October 2023, the Dickinson County Board of Adjustment denied Invenergy a permit to proceed with a proposed 79-turbine wind farm in Dickinson County.

In August 2022, a local resident involved with Tama County Against Turbines Coalition filed a petition for declaratory judgment that the conditional use permits issued by the Tama County Board of Adjustment to Salt Creek Wind were illegal.

In August 2022, the Page County Board of Supervisors approved the 200-MW Shenandoah Hills Wind Farm after 6 months of opposition from residents, who raised concerns about setbacks, noise, lighting, and decommissioning agreements.
Local residents have expressed opposition to MidAmerican’s proposal to construct a 400-MW, 140-turbine wind farm in northern Mills and southern Pottawattamie counties.

The viability of MidAmerican Energy’s plans to construct the 90-turbine Siouxland Wind Farm is in doubt due to Woodbury County’s adoption of an ordinance in August 2022 that increased the setback distance from wind turbines to occupied residences from 1,250 feet to 2,500 feet.

In April 2020, the City Council of Iowa City unanimously voted against a lease agreement with MidAmerican for a solar project in Waterworks Prairie Park due to concern among local residents about the potential damage to the prairie ecosystem.
In 2024, Invenergy proposed the Red Rock Wind Energy Center with a total capacity of 300 MW, two be developed in phases on property in Emmet, Dickinson, Clay Counties (see entry on Dickinson County).
